Why? Unlike traditional plywood you could run the grain the same way on each sheet. Transparent + Transparent = Transparent.

The way that plywood is created is not end grain facing the sides, thus in order to use plywood to achieve that, you'd have to run all of the plies the same direction (so the grain direction went from one side of the panel to the other). At that point, you'd have to either stack a tremendous number of these panels together and bisect them or slice the panel and stack the slices.

The end grain must be facing the viewer for it to be transparent. So if you think of it like straws, you have to be able to see down the inside of the straw, not the side of the straw. I cringe when I see "stronger than x". Is it more resilient under repeated stress? Does it have a higher compressive strength? Is it more scratch-resistant? Will it bend more before breaking? Will it absorb more energy before breaking?

I don't think I've ever seen a new material that's actually stronger by each measure than the thing to which they are comparing it. As such "stronger than x" needs to fall completely out of use.

Also wood was already stronger than glass by many measures.

The other thing is that 'wood' and 'glass' cover a lot of ground. Wood properties vary quite a bit by species and things that fall under the moniker 'glass' these days include Gorilla Glass and synthetic sapphire. Of course this wood isn't really wood at all but just another composite if you replace the lignin with epoxy.
Some expensive hardwoods require a pilot hole for small screws, because the screw head cannot support enough torque to go into the wood.
